question: A rare-earth mine doubles output to meet demand for magnet metals. What happens to its lanthanum and cerium?
options: It doubles too, into a glutted market
It stays level; the mine skips them
It falls as refining favours magnet metals
answer: It doubles too, into a glutted market. The elements sit in the ore in fixed proportions: in bastnäsite, the commonest rare-earth ore, lanthanum and cerium make up roughly three-quarters of the rare earths, neodymium and praseodymium under a fifth. Chasing magnet metals fills warehouses with cheap cerium that nobody ordered.
move: When goods come bundled, demand for one sets the supply of all.
trap: Picturing a mine that can choose which elements it digs up.

diagram.caption: In bastnäsite the magnet metals are under a fifth; every tonne brings mostly cerium and lanthanum.

source: Binnemans & Jones, Journal of Sustainable Metallurgy, 2015
